newsitem.title: USA: TV industry unveils controversial ratings system.
newsitem.headline: TV industry unveils controversial ratings system.

text.p: Television industry executives on Thursday formally unveiled their controversial system to rate programmes, ushering in a new era for TV meant to enable parents to control their kids' viewing habits better.

Broadcast and cable-TV networks will begin displaying the ratings before their shows next month. The age-based system is similar to the 28-year-old motion-picture industry ratings and will apply to all shows except news and sports programmes.

Even before its unveiling, the system had drawn flak from lawmakers, parent groups, children's advocates, educators and others. They want the ratings content-based, specifying the level of sex, violence and strong language.

The ratings cover six categories: TV-G for suitable for all ages; TV-PG for parental guidance suggested; TV-14 for parents of children under 14 strongly cautioned; TV-M for mature audiences only and two categories applying to children's shows: TV-Y for all children and TV-Y7 for kids seven and older.

"This was an effort grounded in honourable purpose. Our goal was to create TV parental guidelines which would be simple to use, easy to understand and handy to find, and we have accomplished it," said Jack Valenti, president of the Motion Picture Association of America and head of the industry group that developed the television ratings.

Networks and distributors will rate their own shows, unlike the movie industry, where an independent panel rates the films. TV executives argue they have far more programmes to rate, with up to 2,000 hours a day of shows, equivalent to about 1,000 movies a day.

Critics, while welcoming the system, say it is vague, does not go far enough and will prove unhelpful to parents. Child advocacy, public health, religious and education groups plan a campaign to see that a content-based system is developed. They favour an approach in which letters such as V, S and L are used to denote the level of violence, sex and bad language.

The ratings stem from the telecommunications law enacted in February that requires new TV sets to include a "V-chip." The technology, expected to be available in a year or so, will be used in conjunction with the ratings and allow parents to screen out programmes they do not want their children to watch.
President Bill Clinton last week gave the system a conditional green light, saying critics should allow the TV industry to test the ratings for 10 months before demanding changes.

Top officials at the Federal Communications Commission will review the ratings over the next several weeks. Under the telecommunications law, the FCC must set up an advisory panel to devise a ratings system if the industry fails within a year to craft an "acceptable" plan.
The TV industry group that developed the system, made up of broadcast, cable-TV and Hollywood executives, vows to fight any government-imposed system in court on First Amendment free speech grounds.
